summary: Alex Karp's attempt to pivot back to the left sparks criticism.
author: The Verge

title: Apple M6 iMac gets fourth refresh; pricey but suits clean‑desk setups
content:
Apple’s latest Apple Silicon iMac, the M6 model, has just entered its fourth refresh. Reviewers note that the device carries a high price tag, yet it remains a solid option for users who value a tidy workspace.

Unlike other Apple Silicon releases that have pushed forward in form factor—such as the more pro‑oriented MacBook Pro, the smaller Mac mini, and the Mac Studio that signals Apple’s shift away from the Mac Pro—the iMac sticks to a classic, thin, screen‑on‑a‑stand design reminiscent of the original Bondi Blue G3 iMac. This aesthetic has made it a common sight in small offices and on television shows that portray compact work environments.

Despite its cost, the iMac’s streamlined appearance and compact footprint still make it a practical choice for those who want a clean desk without sacrificing the performance benefits of Apple Silicon.
summary: The Apple Silicon iMac received its fourth refresh this month, introducing the M6 model. Reviewers say the M6 iMac is pricey but remains a good choice for a clean desk because of its thin, screen‑on‑a‑stand design.
author: Ars Technica

title: Hundreds of streaming services leave viewers saying there is nothing to watch
content: “Fifty-seven channels, and nothin’ on.” Bruce Springsteen famously said those words during a concert and later in a song in the 1990s about the number of TV channels seemingly growing disproportionately to the availability of enjoyable content. Within a few years, there would be hundreds of TV channels and still, some would argue in hyperbolic frustration, “ nothing to watch.” Read full article Comments
summary: Bruce Springsteen famously said “Fifty‑seven channels, and nothin’ on” during a concert and later in a 1990s song about the number of TV channels growing disproportionately to enjoyable content. Within a few years, the number of TV channels rose to hundreds, and some still claim there is nothing to watch.
author: Ars Technica

title: Google, Samsung, Warby Parker launch Gemini smartglasses starting at $395
content:
Google is introducing Gemini‑powered smartglasses that emphasize privacy amid longstanding concerns about wearable cameras. The first models are available for preorder today through eyewear brands Gentle Monster and Warby Parker, marking a collaborative effort that pairs Google’s software with Samsung‑provided computing hardware and designs from the two fashion partners.

Warby Parker offers three frame styles—Alden, Reid and Wren—each in Pine, Saddle and Jet Black finishes, with options for standard optical or sun lenses. Prices start at $395, and sales are limited to the United States. Gentle Monster presents six additional styles in dark‑red, pink, gray and yellow, selectable with clear, tinted, blue or brown lenses; these begin at $449 and will be sold in both the United States and South Korea. The launch follows earlier previews of Google’s “intelligent eyewear” for the Gemini era.
summary: Google, Samsung, Warby Parker and Gentle Monster have released Gemini-powered smartglasses that are now available for preorder. Warby Parker offers three frames (Alden, Reid, Wren) in the US for $395 and higher, while Gentle Monster’s six styles start at $449 and are sold in the US and South Korea.
author: Ars Technica

title: Hot Jupiter TOI-2535b Stops Transiting After Seven Years, Researchers Cite Unseen Companion
content:
Researchers announced that the exoplanet TOI‑2535b, a hot‑Jupiter‑sized world that has been observed transiting its host star TOI‑2535 for roughly seven years, has ceased to appear in transit data. The planet’s regular eclipses had allowed astronomers to use precise timing to study its orbit and to plan observations of its atmosphere.  

The recent disappearance was reported on Monday, and the team proposes that an unseen companion orbiting in a different plane may be responsible for the change in the planet’s observable transits. No further details were provided beyond the suggestion that gravitational influence from this additional body could be altering the transit geometry.
summary: TOI-2535b, a hot Jupiter-sized planet orbiting the star TOI-2535, had been observed transiting for about seven years. Researchers reported that it recently stopped showing up and suspect an unseen companion in a different orbital plane is responsible.
author: Ars Technica

title: Massachusetts man’s secret use of animal testosterone nearly destroyed his heart
content:
A Massachusetts man experienced a decade‑long series of severe health problems, most notably repeated heart failure that required multiple hospitalizations, life‑support treatment, specialist consultations and extensive testing. Throughout this period he did not disclose that he was using powerful, illicit synthetic testosterone derivatives, also known as anabolic‑androgenic steroids (AAS). One of the substances he took was a drug approved solely for animal use, primarily to increase muscle mass in cattle.

Physicians, unaware of his steroid use, had to determine the cause of his condition on their own. A case report describing this investigation appears in this week’s issue of the New England Journal of Medicine. The authors use the case to caution that similar presentations may become more frequent and emphasize the need for clinicians to recognize the signs of illicit AAS use.
summary: A Massachusetts man suffered repeated heart failure and hospitalizations over 11 years while secretly taking illicit synthetic testosterone derivatives, including a drug approved only for use in cattle. Physicians diagnosed the cause and warned that similar cases may become more common.
author: Ars Technica

title: AST SpaceMobile CEO says company will build a 'simple' Blacklift rocket for Bluebird satellites
content: During an hour-long event on Thursday, Abel Avellan, the founder and chief executive of the telecommunications company AST SpaceMobile, laid out his vision for developing a large rocket to launch his Bluebird satellites into orbit. Avellan emphasized, over and over again, that AST plans to build a "simple" rocket. He paraphrased SpaceX founder Elon Musk several times, saying, "the best part is no part." Avellan emphasized that AST has already procured engines for its proposed Blacklift rocket, asserting that engine development accounts for 80 percent of a typical rocket's development cycle. "Of course rocket engineers are going to get mad with me, but you can simplify it as a big tank feeding engines," he said of the rocket. "So big tanks—we know how to do them. We know how to do them. We know how to do them in composite." Read full article Comments
summary: During an hour-long event on Thursday, Abel Avellan, the founder and chief executive of the telecommunications company AST SpaceMobile, laid out his vision for developing a large rocket to launch his Bluebird satellites into orbit. Avellan emphasized, over and over again, that AST plans to build a "simple" rocket.
author: Ars Technica

title: Whoop launches social network for sharing sleep, recovery and workout data
content: Whoop is launching a social network that allows members to share their sleep, recovery and workout data. The company’s broader aim is to evolve into a personal health brand, and CEO Will Ahmed has indicated that acquisitions may follow this shift.
summary: Whoop is launching a social network that lets members share their sleep, recovery, and workout data. CEO Will Ahmed said the company aims to become more of a personal health brand and hinted at future acquisitions.
author: TechCrunch

title: Jensen Huang's ouster from Nvidia may harm AI industry
content: Nvidia’s chief executive Jensen Huang has been ousted, ending a tenure in which he leveraged his influence to advance the artificial‑intelligence sector. The circumstances of his departure, described as more than a typical billionaire scandal, have prompted concerns that his removal could harm the broader AI industry.
summary: Jensen Huang, the ousted CEO of Nvidia, faced a downfall involving a sex scandal. His removal could damage the AI industry because he had been using his influence to push it in specific ways.
author: TechCrunch

title: Jensen Huang agrees to testify before Congress after ouster as CEO
content: Jensen Huang, who was removed as CEO after reports of an alleged affair with a woman suspected of spying for China, has agreed to testify before Congress on Wednesday. His decision follows threats of a subpoena from several senior lawmakers.
summary: Jensen Huang, who was ousted as CEO after reports of an alleged affair with a woman suspected of spying for China, has agreed to testify before Congress. He made the agreement on Wednesday after several senior lawmakers threatened to subpoena him.
author: TechCrunch

title: Phota Labs uses AI to automate editing of everyday photos
content: Phota Labs is applying artificial‑intelligence technology to automate photo editing, allowing users to transform everyday moments into higher‑quality images. The company’s approach focuses on simplifying the editing process rather than adding another conventional photo‑editing tool, aiming to make professional‑looking shots accessible to anyone.
summary: Phota Labs aims to use advances in AI to automate the photo‑editing process. The company says this will make it easier for anyone to turn everyday moments into better photos rather than offering another editing tool.
author: TechCrunch

title: Tanuki: Pon’s Summer review – gentle BMX‑riding raccoon restores a shrine
content:
Tanuki: Pon’s Summer, developed by Denkiworks and Inpleron Limited, is available on Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4 and 5, Xbox One, Series X/S, and PC. The game places the player in the role of a furry post‑office worker who rides a BMX, tasked with repairing an ancient shrine in the weeks before a local festival. Gameplay centers on cleaning trash, mending broken arches and gradually restoring a small rural community.

The review describes the title as a gentle, low‑stakes experience that emphasizes routine and quiet restoration. Its pacing is described as slow and calming, offering a “slow, calming magic” that encourages players to linger despite the game's short length. The reviewer notes that the game’s quiet, steady progress feels well‑suited to the current moment, delivering an intoxicating mix of steady progress and low‑pressure gameplay.
summary: Tanuki: Pon’s Summer is a short, calming game where you play as a BMX‑riding raccoon post‑office worker repairing an ancient shrine and revitalizing a rural community. It is available on Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4/5, Xbox One/Series X/S and PC, and was developed by Denkiworks and Inpleron Limited.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Artists and activists push back against Trump White House’s Arcade video game propaganda
content: Order a Diet Coke or invade Iran – that’s the choice facing the US president in one of several satirical games, as designers turn the gamification of politics back on the White House In early September, the Trump White House announced a surprising new addition to its official website. Named simply Arcade, it is a collection of browser games based on classic titles such as Flappy Bird, Snake, and Tetris, but re-tuned as flagrant works of political propaganda. Designed to court reactionary gamers, they push the administration’s policies on immigration and other hot-button issues, while dehumanising their targets. There have recently been some new additions: a Temple Run clone named Red Scare about crossing the “ration market” and escaping the Democratic Socialists of America, and another simple item-matching game about the threat of socialism. In the midst of increasing fuel, utility and grocery prices thanks to the Iran war, these were naked attempts to distract voters by appealing to their video game nostalgia. After an explosion of news coverage, Arcade caught the attention of the games industry. The Tetris Company warned on social media that it “took copyright infringement very seriously.” Days later, the game was removed from the White House site. However, aside from a March 2026 statement from the Pokémon Company condemning the White House for using its characters in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) propaganda, major video game companies have been relatively silent in the face of the administration’s widespread usage of their IP.
summary: Artists and activists push back against Trump White House’s Arcade video game propaganda.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Notes on the upcoming You’ve Got Mail reboot
content: Substackers in love, dodgy romance scams and Jeff Bezos as the dashing lead … the film-makers behind the remake of the dial-up classic will be facing an embarrassment of pitches Assuming you have already heard about the You’ve Got Mail reboot, you are probably in one of two states. You are either excited that the news might be a signal of a long overdue romcom resurgence, or you are embittered because it’s another sign that Hollywood has run out of original ideas. I hold absolutely no truck with the latter view. Quite frankly, if there was ever a film in dire need of a reboot, then it’s You’ve Got Mail. The film is almost 28 years old, and it shows every single day of its age. You’ve seen it, you know how it goes. It’s about two people who use the futuristic new technology of email (email is no longer new) to communicate, despite being rival booksellers ( nobody reads books any more ), and eventually begin a relationship ( nobody wants to be in a relationship any more ). The whole thing is preposterous. Of course they should try again.
summary: The filmmakers behind the remake of the dial‑up classic “You’ve Got Mail” say they are receiving an embarrassment of pitches, including ideas about Substackers in love, romance scams and Jeff Bezos as the dashing lead. The piece notes the original film is almost 28 years old and argues it is overdue for a reboot.
author: Guardian Technology

title: EcoDataCenter unveils wooden, renewable‑powered datacentre in Falun, Sweden
content:
EcoDataCenter’s new facility in Falun, Sweden, is a datacentre constructed primarily from cross‑laminated timber. The wooden panels arrived pre‑cut and were assembled on site like flat‑pack furniture, giving the building an appearance that the tour guide, John Wernvik, likened to a very large Ikea. The structure, which spans roughly the size of a football pitch, is powered entirely by renewable energy and was designed with the local community in mind.

According to Wernvik, who serves as EcoDataCenter’s chief external relations and sustainability officer, the timber construction reduces the embodied carbon of the building by a factor of three compared with conventional steel‑and‑concrete datacentres. He added that the amount of timber used would take the surrounding Swedish forest about 10 to 15 minutes to regrow, underscoring the facility’s emphasis on rapid renewable resource turnover. The centre is being promoted as potentially the world’s greenest datacentre.
summary: The facility in Falun, Sweden, is a datacentre built of cross‑laminated timber that resembles an Ikea flat‑pack. John Wernvik, EcoDataCenter’s chief external relations and sustainability officer, says the wooden structure lowers embodied carbon threefold and uses timber that regrows in about 10 to 15 minutes of forest growth.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Oakland city workers union authorizes strike to protect jobs from AI
content:
Public employees in Oakland, California, are mobilizing to shape how municipal AI systems are deployed. Concerned that new technologies could expand surveillance and produce inaccurate performance assessments, workers have pressed for safeguards that would prevent layoffs or disciplinary actions driven by AI.

On 22 October, the International Federation of Professional and Technical Engineers Local 21 voted overwhelmingly to authorize a strike, with 94.1 % of members in favor. The union’s action seeks to ensure the city administration adopts a deliberate approach to AI products, rather than implementing tools that may be costly, difficult to manage, or ineffective.

Julian Ware, an Oakland spatial data administrator and union member, said the goal is “to really be intentional about how it’s engaging with AI products,” noting that “sometimes with a fancy new toy, it actually costs more, it’s more difficult to implement and the results are not as good.”
summary: Oakland city workers union authorizes strike to protect jobs from AI.
author: Guardian Technology

title: NHS England removes claim 137 trusts benefit from Palantir AI after 29 report non‑use
content:
NHS England has removed a statement from its website that claimed 137 hospital trusts were benefiting from Palantir’s AI‑powered health data system. The change follows reporting by The Guardian, which found that 29 of the listed trusts were either not live on the platform or were not using any of its applications.

The original NHS communication had presented a list of trusts that were “live” with and “realising benefits” from the federated data platform (FDP), a system intended to improve patient outcomes, operating‑theatre efficiency and the speed of bed discharges. After the discrepancy was highlighted, the list was taken down.
summary: NHS England deleted a claim from its website that 137 hospital trusts are benefiting from Palantir’s AI health data system. The claim was removed after the Guardian reported that 29 of the trusts said the system was not live or they were not using any of its applications.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns amid alleged affairs with Chinese spy and employee
content:
Jensen Huang has stepped down as chief executive of Nvidia after reports surfaced of extramarital affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and a company employee. The resignation follows the admission of these relationships, which have drawn significant attention to the company’s leadership.

Nvidia has named its chief financial officer, Colette Kress, as interim CEO. Kress will serve in the role until a permanent successor is selected.
summary: Jensen Huang has resigned as chief executive of Nvidia after reports of extramarital affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and a company employee. Nvidia’s chief financial officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO until a full-time successor is named.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Slovenia: Red Bull human catapult sets two Guinness World Records
content: Two BASE jumpers were launched from a 360‑metre industrial chimney in Trbovlje, Slovenia, using what organisers called the world’s largest human catapult. The stunt, described as a historic first, earned two Guinness World Records, according to the event’s title.
summary: Two BASE jumpers made history in Trbovlje, Slovenia, after being launched into the sky from a 360-metre industrial chimney using what organisers describe as the world's largest human catapult.
author: Euronews

title: Russian drone strike causes major fire in Kyiv apartment building
content: A Russian drone strike ignited a major fire in an apartment building in Kyiv, Ukraine, early on Thursday. Residents evacuated the building, while firefighters worked to contain the flames and rescue workers provided assistance at the scene.
summary: A Russian drone strike sparked a major fire at an apartment building in Kyiv, Ukraine, early on Thursday. Residents fled to safety as firefighters battled the flames and rescue workers assisted people at the scene.
author: Euronews

title: Russian serviceman killed in Saint Petersburg car explosion
content: A Russian serviceman died after his car exploded in Saint Petersburg on Thursday. Investigators have opened a murder inquiry, and local media say another person was injured in the incident.
summary: A Russian serviceman was killed when his car exploded in Saint Petersburg on Thursday. Investigators have opened a murder inquiry and local media report that another person was injured.
author: Euronews

title: Israeli airstrike hits Nasser Medical Complex in Khan Younis, killing six
content: An Israeli airstrike struck the Nasser Medical Complex in Khan Younis, southern Gaza, early on Thursday, 12 November. The World Health Organization reported that the attack killed six people, including a doctor, and wounded at least 27 others.
summary: An Israeli airstrike struck the Nasser Medical Complex in Khan Younis, southern Gaza, early on Thursday 12 November. The attack killed six people, including a doctor, and injured at least 27 others, according to the World Health Organization.
author: Euronews

title: Gunman kills one in Washington, DC gym shooting, then barricades in building
content: In Washington, DC, a gunman opened fire in a gym, killing one person. After leaving the gym he continued shooting on the street, and police say he subsequently barricaded himself inside a building.
summary: The gunman shot and killed a person inside a gym in Washington, DC. Police said he later fired on the street and barricaded himself inside a building.
author: Euronews

title: “The rules-based international order is breaking down,” Thailand’s Foreign Minister warns
content: Thailand is a “geopolitically safe zone” “in a world where we see the rules based international order breaking down,” Thailand’s Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister tells Euronews in a wide-ranging interview in Bangkok.
summary: Thailand is a “geopolitically safe zone” “in a world where we see the rules based international order breaking down,” Thailand’s Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister tells Euronews in a wide-ranging interview in Bangkok.
author: Euronews

title: France marks 200th anniversary of first permanent photograph
content:
France is marking the 200th anniversary of the first fixed photographic image.  

In a conversation featuring filmmaker Maximilien Van Aertryck and artist Alina Frieske, the camera—described as a “fantastic machine”—is highlighted for enabling passport photos, selfies, award‑winning films, and evening news coverage.
summary: France is celebrating the bicentenary of the first fixed photographic image, marking 200 years of photography. Filmmaker Maximilien Van Aertryck and artist Alina Frieske discuss the image‑obsessed society made possible by the camera.
author: France 24

title: Five shot, one dead in DC neighbourhood near White House; suspect barricaded, then shot himself
content: Police said that early Thursday, at least five people were shot in a Washington, DC neighbourhood near the White House, with one person dying. Officers responded to an apartment building where a suspect was barricaded and later shot himself.
summary: At least one person died after five people were shot early Thursday in a Washington, DC neighbourhood near the White House, police said. Officers responded to a nearby apartment building where a suspect was barricaded and later shot himself.
author: France 24

title: FRANCE 24 tracks Fatemiyoun fighters resurfacing in SE Iran via martyrdom notices
content:
Members of the Fatemiyoun division, a Shia militia, resurfaced in Iran after largely disappearing from public view following the fall of Bashar al‑Assad’s government in Syria in 2024.

FRANCE 24 traced Tehran‑backed Afghan fighters from Syria to southeastern Iran using “martyrdom” announcements and the geolocation of videos shared on social media to track their presence.
summary: Members of the Tehran‑backed Afghan Shia militia Fatemiyoun division have reappeared in Iran after largely disappearing following the fall of Bashar al‑Assad’s government in Syria in 2024. FRANCE 24 traced their presence using “martyrdom” announcements and geolocation of videos shared on social media.
author: France 24

title: Israeli air strike kills six at Gaza's Nasser Hospital, baby dies from cold
content: An overnight Israeli air strike on Nasser Hospital in southern Gaza killed at least six Palestinians, including a teenage boy and a surgeon, according to medics. Elsewhere in Gaza, a nine‑month‑old baby died from the cold as families fled worsening flooding.
summary: An overnight Israeli air strike on Nasser Hospital in southern Gaza killed at least six Palestinians, including a teenage boy and a surgeon. A nine‑month‑old baby died from the cold as families fled worsening flooding in the territory.
author: France 24

title: Putin says Kremlin won’t compromise on Ukraine, offers short ceasefire in key city
content: On Thursday, November 12, President Vladimir Putin told U.S. envoys that the Kremlin would not compromise on its hard‑line demands to end the war in Ukraine, but offered a short‑term ceasefire in a key frontline city. France 24’s International Affairs Editor Philip Turle reports on the meeting.
summary: President Vladimir Putin said on Thursday, November 12 that the Kremlin would not compromise on its hardline demands to end the war in Ukraine. He also offered a short-term ceasefire in a key frontline city during a meeting with US envoys.
author: France 24

title: Nvidia founder Jensen Huang resigns, sparking debate on tech CEOs' influence
content:
The resignation of Nvidia founder Jensen Huang has plunged the company into a leadership crisis, a disruption that is felt beyond Silicon Valley. Nvidia’s role in the rapidly expanding AI industry, where competition between the United States and China is intensifying, makes the upheaval particularly consequential. The immediate focus is on corporate succession, but the event is also sparking a wider conversation about economic resilience, national security, and the political influence of major technology firms.

Trade and economic policy reporter Gavin Bade of The Wall Street Journal notes that the controversy highlights the extraordinary concentration of economic power held by a small number of corporations and their leaders. He questions whether these CEOs wield more authority and influence than elected officials, underscoring the broader debate about the reach of big tech in society.
summary: Jensen Huang, founder of Nvidia, has resigned, creating a leadership crisis at the AI‑focused company. The resignation has prompted discussion, noted by WSJ reporter Gavin Bade, about the concentration of economic power and whether tech CEOs wield more authority than elected officials.
author: France 24

title: France accused of using 2015 anti‑terror law to deter mass protests
content: The French government has been accused of weaponising an anti‑terror law adopted after the 2015 Paris attacks to keep dozens of people away from massive protests sweeping the country. Lawyers and rights groups denounce this as an abuse of power, warning of potentially dangerous repercussions for individual liberties and the right to protest.
summary: The French government has been accused of weaponising an anti‑terror law adopted after the 2015 Paris attacks to keep dozens of people away from massive protests sweeping the country. Lawyers and rights groups say the practice abuses power and threatens individual liberties and the right to protest.
author: France 24

title: Israel bans far-left French politician Jean‑Luc Mélenchon from entry
content: The Israeli government announced on Thursday that it will bar French politician Jean‑Luc Mélenchon from entering Israel. The decision follows Mélenchon’s statement that, if elected president, he would use French vessels to force humanitarian aid into Gaza. The ban was reported a day after France said it had denied entry to the head of an organization representing settlements in the occupied West Bank.
summary: The Israeli government announced on Thursday that it will bar Jean‑Luc Mélenchon from entering Israel. The decision came after Mélenchon said he would use French vessels to force aid into Gaza if elected president.
author: France 24

title: Xi Jinping says reunification with Taiwan inevitable, Taiwan rejects demand
content: China’s leader Xi Jinping reiterated that reunification with Taiwan is inevitable, though he did not refer to the use of military force. Taiwan responded quickly by rejecting Beijing’s demands, and tensions over the island’s future remain ongoing.
summary: Xi Jinping said reunification with Taiwan was inevitable but did not mention military force. Taiwan swiftly rejected Beijing's demands as tensions over the island's future continue.
author: DW World

title: Iranian regime pressures exiled journalists via families, bank accounts and property
content: Exiled Iranian journalists continue to face repression from the Iranian regime. According to the report, leaving the country does not fully free independent reporters, as the government exerts pressure abroad by targeting family members, bank accounts and property left behind.
summary: Independent reporters who have left Iran continue to face repression from the Iranian regime. The regime applies pressure across borders by targeting their family members, bank accounts and property left behind.
author: DW World

title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang steps down after second affair revealed
content: Jensen Huang, credited with building Nvidia into the world’s dominant AI chipmaker, is stepping down as CEO after a second affair was revealed. DW will examine how the loss of its figurehead could affect the company and the broader US‑China AI competition.
summary: Jensen Huang, who built Nvidia into the world’s dominant AI chipmaker, is stepping down as CEO after a second affair came to light. DW examines how losing its figurehead could affect the firm and the US‑China AI race.
author: DW World

title: London court convicts two Iranian citizens of spying on journalists, one for attack plan
content: A London court found two Iranian citizens guilty of surveilling journalists who work for a Persian‑language television station that is critical of Iran’s government. The verdict also included a conviction for one of the men on a separate charge of planning a violent attack against those reporters.
summary: A London court found two Iranian citizens guilty of surveilling reporters for a Persian‑language television station critical of Iran's government. One of the men was also convicted of planning a violent attack against the journalists.
author: DW World

title: Hungary eases abortion restrictions, scrapping heartbeat regulation
content: Hungary is easing abortion restrictions as part of a broader overhaul of women’s rights. The reforms break with the conservative policies of former prime minister Viktor Orban, scrapping the controversial “heartbeat regulation” and extending greater protection for women against violence.
summary: The reforms mark a break with the conservative policies of former PM Viktor Orban. The controversial “heartbeat regulation” will be scrapped and women will be better protected against violence.
author: DW World

title: Ukraine, US, Russia hold first trilateral talks in nine months, agree prisoner swap
content: The first trilateral talks in nine months between Ukraine, the United States and Russia, held in Abu Dhabi, concluded with an agreement to exchange prisoners. This prisoner‑exchange arrangement is the only concrete outcome reported from the meeting.
summary: The first trilateral talks between Ukraine, the US and Russia in nine months were held in Abu Dhabi. The talks ended with an agreement to exchange prisoners.
author: DW World

title: EU proposes Digital Fairness Act to curb subscription traps and misleading online tactics
content: The European Union is preparing a Digital Fairness Act aimed at reducing subscription traps, misleading sales tactics and design features that encourage endless scrolling. The proposal seeks to make it more difficult for online platforms to deceive consumers, though observers are questioning whether the measures go far enough to protect users.
summary: The EU wants to curb subscription traps, misleading sales tactics and features that keep people scrolling through the proposed Digital Fairness Act. It examines what the Digital Fairness Act would change and whether it goes far enough.
author: DW World

title: UK car industry seeks two-year EU delay on Brexit EV tariffs
content:
The UK car industry is preparing to push the European Union for a two‑year delay to the implementation of Brexit tariffs on electric vehicles traded between the UK and the EU.  

This follows an initial EU proposal that suggested a shorter delay. The rules of origin on vehicle batteries are set to take effect on 1 January, unless the two sides reach a new agreement to postpone the rules for a second time.
summary: The UK car industry is preparing to push the EU for a two‑year delay to Brexit tariffs on electric cars. The tariffs and related battery “rules of origin” are set to take effect on 1 January unless an agreement is reached.
author: Guardian World

title: Greta Thunberg says planet is being killed at Cop31 climate summit
content: Swedish activist criticised world governments for their failure to prevent environmental breakdown The planet is “not dying, it is being killed and we know by who”, said Greta Thunberg, who excoriated world governments for their failure to prevent environmental breakdown in her first appearance at the annual UN climate talks in five years. Thunberg, 23, the Swedish activist who became famous for heading the school climate strike movement, delivered her stark message to those gathered at the Cop31 summit in Antalya, Turkey, amid the ongoing failure by countries to adequately address the climate crisis.
summary: Greta Thunberg says planet is being killed at Cop31 climate summit.
author: Guardian World

title: Finland bans Russian athletes from entering over Ukraine war
content:
Finland announced that it will restrict entry to the country for Russian athletes because of the war in Ukraine, with skating and cross‑country skiing identified as the first sports to be affected. The decision follows a backlash in Finland after Russia was reinstated for the ice‑hockey world championships.

Foreign Affairs Minister Elina Valtonen said, “As long as Russia’s war of aggression continues, Russian athletes have no business in Finland,” adding that their entry would threaten Finland’s international relations. She also stated that short‑term work under visas that is not essential to Finland’s national interests would be treated similarly.
summary: Finland will restrict entry to the country for Russian athletes because of the war in Ukraine, which could affect several winter sports. Foreign Affairs Minister Elina Valtonen said Russian athletes have no business in Finland while the war continues, viewing their entry as a threat to international relations and non‑essential short‑term work visas.
author: Guardian World

title: Putin warns US Russia will target foreign troops in Ukraine, refuses territorial concessions
content:
At a Kremlin meeting with U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff on Thursday, President Vladimir Putin warned that Russia would target any foreign troops sent to Ukraine. He also refused to soften his territorial demands, insisting on full control of the four Ukrainian regions Moscow says it has annexed.

The hard‑line statements came as the Ukrainian military reported renewed disruptions to Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite service.
summary: Putin warned US negotiators Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff that Russia would target any foreign troops sent to Ukraine. He also refused to soften territorial demands, insisting on full control of four Ukrainian regions claimed as annexed, as Ukraine reported renewed disruptions to Starlink service.
author: Guardian World

title: Labor party runs NSW news Instagram account, expert warns communication loophole
content: Expert warns of ‘huge loophole in political communication laws’ as state government among parties presenting accounts as unaffiliated news sources Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast “Breaking,” a reel from the Instagram account nswnewsroom reads. “Another Liberal MP quits, almost a third now gone.” The post looks like it could have been made by a media outlet. It cites the source as the Daily Telegraph and Jordan Lane, a New South Wales MP, who is the sixth sitting Liberal member to announce they won’t re-contest their seat at the March 2027 election. Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here
summary: Labor party runs NSW news Instagram account, expert warns communication loophole.
author: Guardian World

title: ICAC inquiry finds NSW ‘guns for hire’ network, major parties resist reform
content:
The New South Wales Independent Commission Against Corruption (Icac) revealed in its recent Rosny inquiry that a group of right-wing Liberal operatives, known as the Reformers, operated with significant ease within NSW parliament. These former staffers were involved in various activities, including peddling a dirt file on a state minister to journalists, conducting a subterranean campaign to discredit the building commissioner, and convincing the Liberal party to unseat councillors in the Hills district who were blocking a developer.

The inquiry highlights the state’s “guns for hire” problem. While Premier Chris Minns is attempting to address the threat of undeclared lobbying, the report indicates his efforts fall well short of the recommendations made by the commission five years ago. Consequently, neither major party appears serious about implementing the necessary reforms.
summary: Chris Minns is trying to address the threat of undeclared lobbying but falls well short of what the commission recommended five years ago Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast A dirt file on a state minister peddled to journalists. A subterranean campaign to discredit the building commissioner.
author: Guardian World

title: Australia sees surge in teen extremism as 32 of 37 counter‑terror cases involve under‑18s
content: Young people are being found with ‘hard drives full of what can only be described as gore’, one expert says In March, Guardian Australia revealed that most people who have been charged with the new federal crime of possession of violent extremist material are under 18. This week Australian federal police sounded the alarm about a surge in teen extremism: 32 of the 37 young people prosecuted in counter-terrorism cases since 2020 were charged in the past two years.
summary: Australia sees surge in teen extremism as 32 of 37 counter‑terror cases involve under‑18s.
author: Guardian World

title: Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza cleared of AI use in Caine prize win
content: After a month-long investigation it was concluded that Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which won the £10,000 Caine prize, was ‘human-written’ The Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza has been cleared of using AI to write a prize-winning short story, after the prestigious Caine prize for African writers concluded that his entry was “human-written” after a month-long investigation. Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which charts the declining fortunes of a family after the father invests in fish tanks, was announced as the winner of the £10,000 prize on 6 October.
summary: After a month‑long investigation the Caine prize panel concluded Kundizeza’s story “The Blue Fighter” was human‑written. The short story was announced as the winner of the £10,000 prize on 6 October.
author: Guardian World

title: SpaceX launches classified USSF-627 mission from Vandenberg
content:
SpaceX launched a classified mission for the U.S. Space Force on November 11, marking the second such flight for the company in a six-day period. The Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California at 11:36 p.m. EST, initiating a mission designated USSF-627. This launch followed a similar liftoff on November 6, when a Falcon 9 sent the USSF-432 mission skyward from the same central coast site. Both missions remain classified, and SpaceX did not reveal specific details about their payloads. While experts have speculated that these flights may have deployed Starshield satellites for the Space Force’s Space Based Sensing and Targeting portfolio, no official confirmation has been provided.

In both instances, SpaceX ended the webcast shortly after the Falcon 9 first stages returned to Earth. The boosters landed on the SpaceX drone ship "Of Course I Still Love You," stationed in the Pacific Ocean downrange of Vandenberg, approximately 8.5 minutes after liftoff. The booster used for the USSF-627 mission, designated 1103, completed its seventh flight. Previous missions for this booster included NROL-179, SDA-T1TL-E, SDA-T1TL-A, and three Starlink deployments.

The USSF-627 launch was the 120th Falcon 9 mission of 2026 and the rocket’s 15th national-security flight of the year. Of the 120 total flights in 2026, 85 were dedicated to expanding SpaceX’s Starlink broadband constellation, which currently comprises more than 11,000 satellites in low Earth orbit. The current launch cadence is lower than the previous year; in 2025, the Falcon 9 conducted 165 missions, with 122 of those flights supporting Starlink.
summary: SpaceX launches classified USSF-627 mission from Vandenberg.
author: Space.com

title: Japan FA Honorary President Kozo Tashima Aims to Quietly Challenge Infantino
content:
Kozo Tashima, the honorary president of the Japan Football Association, is running as a challenger to Fifa president Gianni Infantino. The 68-year-old is described as an unlikely insurgent who aims to shift the organization away from controversial headlines toward a calmer era focused on listening. Tashima, a respected figure in Asian and global football politics, is pursuing this bid independently.

His candidacy follows Japan’s unsuccessful bid for the 2022 World Cup, where the country finished with only two of the final 22 votes. Tashima was involved in that earlier campaign and is now hoping that a quieter approach will be welcomed by the football community as he seeks to topple the current president.
summary: Kozo Tashima, the 68‑year‑old honorary president of the Japan Football Association, is seeking to oust Gianni Infantino from the FIFA presidency. He hopes a calmer, quieter approach will replace the headlines that have dominated FIFA’s recent history, leveraging his reputation as a respected figure in Asian and global football politics.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Shoaib Bashir’s algorithmic magic fizzles amid Test spin decline
content:
Shoaib Bashir was left out of England’s squad for the South Africa tour, a decision that the author notes signals a shift in the sport toward the demands of T20 cricket and the use of hard data.  

During the summer, Sky Sports ran a commercial featuring England players Harry Brook and Jacob Bethell. The ad began with a generic male voiceover about diversifying forex contingents and then cut to the players performing staged cricketing feats.  

The sequence culminated when Bashir stepped onto the field to bowl his trademark off‑break with a high release point. Bethell then stepped down the track, struck the Wealth Centaur‑branded ball, and shattered a CGI wall, sending the ball into a hail of digital rain.  

The author interprets Bashir’s omission and the ad’s focus on data‑driven, short‑format cricket as evidence of a broader change in how Test spin is valued within the game.
summary: Shoaib Bashir was left out of the squad to tour South Africa, highlighting a sport reshaped by the needs of T20 and hard data. His algorithmic magic fizzles, echoing a wider decline of Test spin.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Harry Kane to become England's most capped player with 126 appearances
content:
Harry Kane is set to play his historic 126th international match against Croatia at Wembley, a game that will make him England’s most capped player. The striker’s appearance count will bring him level with notable figures such as Dani Alves, Eden Hazard and Paolo Maldini, each of whom also have 126 caps.

Despite reaching this milestone, Kane’s total remains modest when viewed against the broader history of international football. Players like Kevin De Bruyne and Luís Figo have already reached 127 caps, while Manuel Neuer has 128. Consequently, it will be some time before Kane climbs into European football’s top‑50 list for international appearances, let alone the global rankings.
summary: Harry Kane will become England's most capped player when he plays his 126th match against Croatia at Wembley. His 126 caps tie him with players such as Dani Alves, Eden Hazard and Paolo Maldini, but he is not yet in the top 50 European or global capped players.
author: Guardian Sport

title: UK Sport launches Sport Org, sparking concerns among governing bodies
content:
The recent establishment of Sport Org by UK Sport has sparked concern among governing bodies, with smaller sports fearing potential takeover. The move is seen as a significant change that is ruffling feathers and stoking fears within the Olympic and Paralympic community.

Sport Org evolved from British Curling and now employs its leaders and expertise across several disciplines, including curling, para‑curling, para table tennis, squash, and, starting in 2030, bobsleigh and skeleton.
summary: UK Sport has created a new body called Sport Org, which evolved from British Curling. The organisation will use its leaders and expertise across curling, para‑curling, para table tennis, squash and, from 2030, bobsleigh and skeleton, sparking concerns among smaller sports about potential takeover.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Jimmy Anderson signs with Surrey for 2027
content: Veteran bowler was released by Lancashire ‘I can’t wait to start a new chapter in my career’ Jimmy Anderson will continue his career in 2027 after signing to play for Surrey. England men’s all-time leading wicket taker was released by Lancashire at the end of the 2026 season. But the 44-year-old will play on after agreeing a deal at the Kia Oval. More to follow
summary: Veteran bowler Jimmy Anderson, 44, was released by Lancashire at the end of the 2026 season. The England men's all-time leading wicket taker has signed a deal to play for Surrey at the Kia Oval in 2027.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Barcelona's 'Barca Way' Persists in Women's Champions League vs Arsenal
content: Arsenal face a much-changed Barcelona in the Women's Champions League on Thursday - but how have the Spanish giants coped so well with losing key players?
summary: Arsenal will face a much-changed Barcelona in the Women's Champions League on Thursday. Despite losing key players, Barcelona has coped well.
author: BBC Sport

title: Scotland captain Andy Robertson poised to equal Kenny Dalglish caps record
content: Scotland captain Andy Robertson is poised to make history by matching Kenny Dalglish’s record for international caps, a milestone highlighted by writer Tom English. English notes that the two men share a bond that extends beyond the numbers, linking them in more ways than one.
summary: Scotland captain Andy Robertson is set to match Kenny Dalglish's caps record. Tom English notes the strong ties between Robertson and his hero Dalglish.
author: BBC Sport

title: Trump administration unveils plan to sell public lands to states, localities and tribes
content: The Trump administration announced this week that it plans to sell portions of public lands in the coming years. According to a new strategic plan for the Interior Department covering 2026 onward, the agency will work to reduce the federal estate by offering states, localities and Tribes the chance to purchase federal lands.
summary: The Trump administration announced a plan to sell some public lands in the years ahead. The Interior Department said the plan will work to decrease the federal estate by offering states, localities and Tribes the opportunity to purchase federal lands.
author: The Hill

title: The Memo: Misfire on Hegseth vote adds to Democratic tensions
content: Democrats acknowledge they fumbled Tuesday by allowing House Republicans to block an effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. The incident has sparked debate over whether the failure reflects isolated disorganization or a broader issue. Progressives express irritation that extends beyond the specific details of the impeachment vote’s collapse.
summary: Democrats admit they fumbled Tuesday when they allowed House Republicans to block an effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Now the question is whether the embarrassing misfire can be chalked up to one-off disorganization or is symptomatic of a larger problem.
author: The Hill

title: Palantir’s Karp says he’s been criticizing Trump on immigration ‘in private’
content: Palantir CEO Alex Karp revealed he has been criticizing President Trump “in private” over his handling of immigration and the administration detaining a record number of people throughout the summer. “Well, I’m really happy to hear the president, you know, in his words: ‘yeah, we kind of went too far,” Karp told Politico’s Adam Wren.…
summary: Palantir’s Karp says he’s been criticizing Trump on immigration ‘in private’.
author: The Hill

title: Rep. Robert Garcia Discusses 2027 Oversight Plans and White House Response
content: NPR correspondent A Martinez interviewed California Democratic Representative Robert Garcia, the incoming House Oversight Committee chair, regarding his 2027 plans to investigate the Trump administration. The discussion also covered the White House’s response to these proposed investigations.
summary: Democratic Rep. Robert Garcia of California discussed plans for the 2027 House Oversight Committee to investigate the Trump administration. He also addressed the White House response to these proposed investigations.
author: NPR Politics

title: Michigan Senator-elect El Sayed discusses Democrats' ambitions
content:
NPR’s Leila Fadel interviewed U. S. Senator‑elect Abdul El‑Sayed (D‑Mich.) about his victory in the midterms.  
El‑Sayed outlined the priorities that will guide his first term in Congress, emphasizing the issues he plans to address once he takes office.
summary: Michigan Senator-elect El Sayed discusses Democrats' ambitions.
author: NPR Politics

title: Supreme Court weakens Voting Rights Act; blue wave stalls Black House decline
content: A Supreme Court ruling that weakened the Voting Rights Act set the stage for a record decline in Black representation in the U.S. House. However, a midterm blue wave temporarily offset this trend, preventing the anticipated drop in Black members of Congress.
summary: A Supreme Court ruling that weakened the Voting Rights Act paved the way for a record drop in Black representation in Congress. A midterm blue wave helped hold off that decline for now.
author: NPR Politics

title: Burnham's push for closer EU ties causes ripples in his party and others
content: The Prime Minister’s stance on Europe is prompting MPs to consider their leaders’ individual strategies. This occurs ahead of a week focused on the UK’s relationship with the EU bloc.
summary: Ahead of a week which will focus minds on the UK's relationship with the bloc, the prime minister's stance on Europe is causing MPs to think about their leaders' individual strategy.
author: BBC Politics

title: COP31 Climate Talks in Turkey: How Far Off Target Are We?
content: Heads of government are convening in Turkey for the next fortnight to conduct the latest round of climate talks, amid concerns about unprecedented human‑caused global heating. In a video interview, Madeleine Finlay explains to co‑host Ian Sample why these negotiations are critical and discusses the chances of achieving meaningful change.
summary: Heads of government are meeting in Turkey for the next fortnight for the latest round of climate talks. Madeleine Finlay discusses the importance of the negotiations and the chances of meaningful change with co-host Ian Sample.
author: Guardian Environment

title: World heading for ‘irrevocable overshoot’ of global temperature thresholds, analysis warns
content:
A new analysis from Climate Action Tracker (CAT) warns that the world is moving toward an “irrecoverable overshoot” of global temperature thresholds. The report states that continued failure to reduce emissions will consign humanity to disasters that it cannot adapt to, citing the prolonged delay by governments in cutting planet‑heating emissions.

According to CAT, current policies will raise global temperatures by an average of 2.7 °C above preindustrial levels by the end of the century. This projection is slightly higher than the 2.6 °C estimate made in the group’s analysis the previous year.
summary: World heading for ‘irrevocable overshoot’ of global temperature thresholds, analysis warns.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Ofwat to tighten water industry bonus ban after Anglian Water makes £800k retention payment
content: Regulator to hasten review over concerns that firms are ‘undermining’ rules to make large payments to bosses Business live – latest updates The water company bonus ban is set to be tightened after the regulator accused the industry of a risk of “damaging public trust” with large payments to bosses that appeared to get around the rules. Anglian Water was singled out for particular criticism over “retention payments” worth up to £800,000 for chief executive Mark Thurston despite the bonus ban. Anglian will face increased monitoring of its governance arrangements because of the controversial payments.
summary: Ofwat said it will tighten the water industry bonus ban after warning that large payments to executives risk damaging public trust. Anglian Water was singled out for making up to £800,000 in retention payments to chief executive Mark Thurston and will face increased monitoring of its governance arrangements.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Cop31: “No one is coming to rescue us” Greta Thunberg tells climate summit
content: World leaders including UK prime minister Andy Burnham are addressing the summit today, as talks head into the third day Zack Polanski, leader of the Green party in the UK, criticised Andy Burnham’s Cop31 speech on Radio 4’s Today programme. Saying he was “not at all reassured” by the prime minister’s words, he described it as a “bizarre” speech. Polanski said climate action is about what you do, not what you say, referring to the recent decision by the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, to allow drilling in the Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea. It’s “one step forwards, two steps back”, Polanski said.
summary: Cop31: “No one is coming to rescue us” Greta Thunberg tells climate summit.
author: Guardian Environment

title: SS United States Sinks Off Destin, Florida, to Become Largest Artificial Reef
content:
The SS United States, a historic U.S. ocean liner, sank off the coast of Destin, Florida, on Wednesday.  

The nearly 1,000‑foot, American‑made vessel was launched in 1952 and set a transatlantic speed record on its maiden voyage. It carried thousands of passengers across the Atlantic during 17 years of service before retiring in 1969.  

The ship will now serve as the world’s largest artificial reef.
summary: The SS United States, a nearly 1,000‑foot American‑made ocean liner launched in 1952, sank off the coast of Destin, Florida, Wednesday. It will become the world’s largest artificial reef after its retirement in 1969 and its 17‑year service carrying thousands of passengers across the Atlantic.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Francis Crick Institute tests thousands of BRCA1 variants for breast cancer risk
content: Researchers at the Francis Crick Institute have tested thousands of possible BRCA1 mutations in mammary gland cells to identify which genetic variants confer a high risk of developing breast cancer. The study aims to improve future interpretation of genetic test results.
summary: Researchers at the Francis Crick Institute tested thousands of BRCA1 mutations in mammary gland cells to determine which variants carry a high breast cancer risk. The study may improve future interpretation of genetic test results.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Researchers develop low-cost blood test for early detection of rheumatic heart disease
content: Rheumatic heart disease kills hundreds of thousands annually, particularly affecting children and young adults in low- and middle-income countries. These regions often lack specialized ultrasound equipment and refrigerated testing labs. Although inexpensive penicillin can halt progressive valve damage if the disease is detected early, millions remain undiagnosed until irreversible heart failure occurs.
summary: Researchers have designed a low-cost blood test for rheumatic heart disease that can be used in resource-poor clinics. Early detection with the test could allow inexpensive penicillin to stop valve damage before irreversible heart failure sets in, addressing the millions of undiagnosed cases that cause hundreds of thousands of deaths each year.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Study Finds Patients at Risk from NHS-Private Hospital Quality Gaps
content: Researchers from the universities of York, Manchester and Birmingham have found that while NHS and private hospitals each have internal systems to assure the quality and safety of care, these systems do not operate effectively across organisational boundaries. The study highlights that patients may be at risk of quality failures when care transitions between NHS and private settings.
summary: Researchers from the universities of York, Manchester and Birmingham discovered that quality and safety assurance systems exist within NHS and private hospitals. However, these systems do not work well between organizations.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Survey: Most Americans on High Alert for Foodborne Illnesses Amid 2026 Food Recalls
content: A survey indicates most Americans are on higher alert for foodborne illnesses amid an unprecedented 2026 year of food recalls. The year has seen unusually high outbreak case counts and recall volume by weight, prompting Americans to take precautions during the holiday season to protect their families.
summary: The year 2026 has seen unusually severe food safety issues, with high outbreak case counts and large recall volumes. Americans are on high alert to protect their loved ones during the holiday season.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Blood test may identify advanced prostate cancer patients who benefit from targeted radiotherapy
content: Researchers from The Royal Marsden NHS Foundation Trust, The Institute of Cancer Research in London, and University College London have reported that a blood test may identify men with advanced prostate cancer who are more likely to achieve longer disease control following targeted radiotherapy. The findings were published in JAMA Network Open.
summary: A blood test could help identify men with advanced prostate cancer who are more likely to experience longer disease control after targeted radiotherapy. The research was led by The Royal Marsden NHS Foundation Trust, The Institute of Cancer Research, London and University College London, and published in JAMA Network Open.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Nigeria gradually expands malaria vaccine rollout to households
content: Nigeria is rolling out a malaria vaccine slowly, administering it house by house. In one session, a needle broke the skin, prompting wailing and a reassuring “sorry, sorry” from the medical staff; the baby was then vaccinated against malaria, a disease that remains an intractable child killer in Nigeria.
summary: Nigeria is slowly rolling out a malaria vaccine across households. Medical staff administer the injection to babies, apologizing as they vaccinate.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Irregular sleep schedules linked to higher anxiety, depression and loneliness, study finds
content: A large study conducted by researchers at the University of California, San Francisco and the University of California, San Diego found that individuals with irregular sleep‑wake schedules may experience heightened symptoms of anxiety, depression and loneliness. The findings suggest a link between erratic sleep patterns and poorer mental‑health outcomes.
summary: People with irregular sleep-wake schedules may experience more severe symptoms of anxiety, depression and loneliness. The findings come from a large study led by UC San Francisco and UC San Diego.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Una Brown saves husband Sean and a stranger by donating kidney in indirect manner
content: Una Brown, who had previously said she would donate a kidney to her husband Sean if necessary, carried out a kidney donation in a roundabout manner that she says saved both a stranger’s life and her husband’s at the same time.
summary: Una Brown said she would donate a kidney to her husband Sean if needed. She ultimately saved both Sean and a stranger by providing a kidney in an indirect manner.

title: War in Ukraine and Middle East fuels talk of possible third world war
content: Commentators note that ongoing conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East have sparked renewed speculation about the possibility of a third world war. The discussion centers on how to define a “global” war, questioning what criteria make a conflict truly worldwide.
summary: War in Ukraine and Middle East fuels talk of possible third world war.

title: Summer drought from Romania to Kazakhstan linked to reduced winter ice in warming seas
content: The title notes that summer droughts spanning from Romania to Kazakhstan are linked to reduced winter ice in two rapidly warming seas. This summer experienced scarce rainfall and repeated heat waves, producing one of Europe’s most severe droughts since 1540. Wildfires in western Europe attracted media attention, while eastern Europe also suffered heavily, worsening the humanitarian crisis caused by the war in Ukraine. Simulations indicate that such droughts are expected to become more frequent and severe in the future because of man‑made global warming.
summary: This summer, with its scarce rainfall and repeated heat waves, witnessed one of the most severe droughts in Europe since 1540. The resulting wildfires across western Europe received considerable media attention, but eastern Europe was also heavily hit, worsening the humanitarian crisis caused by the war in Ukraine.

title: ISC researchers find potentials and electric fields jointly influence electrochemical reactions
content: Researchers in the Interface Science Department (ISC) have demonstrated that electrochemical reactions occurring at solid‑solution interfaces are influenced by two distinct factors. An applied electric potential can directly drive a reaction forward, while electric fields present in the surrounding environment can alter the ensembles that set activation parameters, even though those fields do not themselves provide a thermodynamic driving force.
summary: Researchers at the Interface Science Department (ISC) showed that an applied potential can drive electrochemical reactions at solid‑solution interfaces. They also found that electric fields in the extended environment can modulate the ensembles determining activation parameters without providing a thermodynamic driving force.

content: Baboons have taken up residence in Simon’s Town, prompting a long‑standing split among residents. Defenders of the animals and those opposed to them have been at odds, confronting each other on social‑media platforms and, at times, in person for years.

content: Swiss researchers have identified a new method for detecting the date‑rape drug GHB in urine for up to 72 hours after ingestion. The technique could provide a useful tool for sexual‑assault investigations.

content: A 20th‑century US ocean liner that previously carried royal leaders, movie stars and the “Mona Lisa” to the United States was deliberately sunk on Wednesday. The sinking is intended to create the world’s largest artificial reef.

title: Light-controlled tool stops autophagy, providing clues to disease mechanisms
content: A newly described light‑controlled tool can temporarily stop autophagy, the cellular recycling process that breaks down worn‑out components for reuse, providing researchers with clues about disease mechanisms. The tool’s ability to halt this essential pathway under precise illumination offers a way to study how disruptions in autophagy may contribute to pathology. Christina Towers, Ph.D., is identified as an expert on autophagy, the recycling system targeted by the light‑activated approach.
summary: Inside each cell is a dynamic world of molecules and chemicals, signals and receivers, and construction and destruction. With all this activity, it's inevitable that cellular parts get worn down over time.

title: MIT researchers develop synthetic-data technique to speed up climate AI models
content:
MIT researchers have introduced a new training technique that speeds the creation of climate‑prediction AI models, known as climate emulators, while boosting their reliability and adaptability. The method, detailed in a paper published this week in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, uses only a fraction of the data traditionally required to train an emulator. By generating a small, carefully selected set of synthetic climate scenarios, the team shows that the resulting emulator can accurately predict outcomes of scenarios it has never seen during training—something that conventional emulators struggle to achieve.

Climate emulators are designed to mimic the behavior of full‑scale Earth system models (ESMs), which simulate global temperature and precipitation changes in great detail but can take months to run on supercomputers. In contrast, emulators can produce results in seconds, enabling scientists to test thousands of policy‑relevant scenarios quickly. However, building an emulator typically involves running six to eight realistic future scenarios through an ESM, a costly and time‑consuming process. The new algorithm replaces these realistic runs with synthetic data that contains rapid, high‑frequency variations in emissions, such as dramatic increases in CO₂ in 2050 or sharp decreases in methane in 2037. These “wiggles” provide the emulator with a richer information set, improving its predictive skill across a broader range of conditions.

Lead author Christoher Womack, a postdoc at ETH Zurich, explained that the algorithm iteratively updates the training data until the emulator’s error falls below a chosen threshold. The approach requires running the full ESM only once, dramatically cutting production time. Womack noted that emulators trained with this technique can capture the effects of local pollutant‑control policies—an area where traditional emulators failed.

The research team, which includes Shahine Bouabid, Andrei Sokolov, Popat Salunke, Glenn Flierl, Sebastian D. Eastham, and senior author Noelle E. Selin, plans to test the method with scenarios generated by a full ESM and to apply it to other climate models. The work is part of the Bringing Computation to the Climate Challenge (BC3) project and was supported by Schmidt Sciences through the MIT Grand Challenges.
summary: MIT researchers developed a training technique that uses a small set of synthetic climate scenarios to train AI climate emulators, cutting the data needed and speeding production. The emulators can quickly simulate climate impacts and adapt to novel scenarios, improving reliability for policy decisions.
author: MIT News

title: Scientists find early land animals had stiff necks, not for head turning
content: Scientists have found that the earliest animals to colonize land about 380 million years ago possessed surprisingly stiff necks, challenging a long‑standing evolutionary theory. The new research suggests necks did not develop to aid head turning but likely arose alongside anatomical changes that enabled movement with the front limbs.
summary: Scientists have discovered that the first animals to venture onto land nearly 380 million years ago had surprisingly stiff necks. The finding overturns the theory that necks evolved to help animals turn their heads, suggesting instead they arose as part of anatomical changes enabling front‑limb movement.
author: Science Daily

title: NASA Parker Solar Probe finds magnetic fields reverse rotation at tiny scales
content:
NASA’s Parker Solar Probe discovered a hidden pattern in the Sun’s chaotic magnetic fields. It found that turbulent magnetic fields reverse their direction of rotation when examined at extremely small scales.

This unexpected pattern in solar wind turbulence could help scientists better understand solar activity and predict geomagnetic storms.
summary: NASA’s Parker Solar Probe found that turbulent magnetic fields reverse their direction of rotation at extremely small scales. The discovery reveals an unexpected pattern in solar wind turbulence that could help scientists better understand solar activity and predict geomagnetic storms.
author: Science Daily

title: Researchers build quantum computer that stores data via microscopic vibrations
content: Researchers have built a quantum computer that stores information in microscopic vibrations. This approach could make quantum machines smaller, more powerful, and better at preserving information. The breakthrough successfully demonstrated advanced quantum calculations and may help overcome major barriers to practical quantum computing.
summary: Researchers have created a quantum computer that stores information in microscopic vibrations. The device demonstrated advanced quantum calculations and may help overcome major barriers to practical quantum computing.
author: Science Daily

title: Lumina simulation maps 2 billion years of early universe across 1.6 billion light‑years
content: A new supercomputer simulation named Lumina is shedding light on how the universe emerged from its cosmic dark age and formed stars and galaxies. The simulation models two billion years of early cosmic history over a 1.6‑billion‑light‑year region, providing unprecedented detail beyond earlier simulations.
summary: A new supercomputer simulation named Lumina is revealing how the universe escaped its cosmic dark age and became filled with stars and galaxies. Lumina recreates two billion years of early cosmic history across a region 1.6 billion light‑years wide, showing details beyond earlier simulations.
author: Science Daily

title: Study suggests Earth's fiery atmosphere could have produced hundreds of oceans of water
content: Scientists have discovered that during Earth’s early formation, rocky pebbles reacting with hydrogen under extreme heat can produce water in minutes. This reaction, occurring in the planet’s fiery atmosphere, could have generated hundreds of oceans’ worth of water while Earth was still forming. The findings suggest that water may be a natural component of how rocky planets form, rather than something that must arrive from comets or asteroids.
summary: Earth's water may have been born in the planet's fiery atmosphere rather than delivered by icy comets or asteroids. Scientists discovered that rocky pebbles reacting with hydrogen under extreme heat can produce water in minutes, potentially generating hundreds of oceans' worth during Earth's formation.
author: Science Daily

title: Study: football, handball raise bone formation markers up to 46% vs walking
content:
A surprising new study suggests that walking, jogging, and even traditional weight training may be less effective at stimulating bone formation than high‑intensity sports involving explosive movements and sudden changes in direction.  

Researchers found that activities such as football and handball increased markers of bone formation by up to 46%, potentially revealing a better way to protect bones against aging and osteoporosis.
summary: Researchers found that walking, jogging and traditional weight training were less effective at stimulating bone formation than high‑intensity sports with explosive movements and sudden direction changes. Activities such as football and handball increased markers of bone formation by up to 46%, suggesting a potentially better way to protect bones against aging and osteoporosis.
author: Science Daily

title: Study finds fructose may aid spread of aggressive ovarian cancer
content: Scientists have found that fructose, a sugar common in sweetened foods and drinks, can aid the spread of aggressive ovarian cancer. In laboratory studies, cancer cells that survive chemotherapy were observed to release fructose, which weakens the connections between neighboring tumor cells and makes it easier for the disease to disseminate. The same preclinical experiments also showed that high dietary fructose levels and the use of cholesterol‑lowering statins produced similarly concerning effects on cancer cell behavior.
summary: Researchers found that chemotherapy‑surviving aggressive ovarian cancer cells release fructose that weakens the bonds between neighboring tumor cells, making spread easier. High dietary fructose levels and cholesterol‑lowering statins produced concerning effects in preclinical experiments.
author: Science Daily

title: NIH study links two forever chemicals to 93% higher aggressive breast cancer risk
content: An NIH study reported that women with elevated concentrations of two common “forever chemicals” experienced up to a 93% increase in rates of an aggressive form of breast cancer. The finding highlights concerns about the potential health impacts of persistent chemicals present in everyday products.
summary: An NIH study found that women with high levels of two common forever chemicals had up to 93% higher rates of an aggressive form of breast cancer. The finding raises concerns about the potential health effects of persistent chemicals found in everyday products.
author: Science Daily

content: Madeleine Finlay and co-host Ian Sample discuss the three science stories you need to know about this week, including an alternative to BMI for diagnosing obesity which could ‘prevent misdiagnosis for millions’. Also on the agenda: an update from this year’s Cop climate conference in Turkey, and a study that claims to have found the key to better conversations with the help of a concept from physics Follow the Guardian’s coverage of Cop31 Want to have a better chat? Scientists say the secret is ‘pink noise’
